title: Test-Space Training: Learning Specialized Representations from Multimodal Data in One Place
one_liner: Instead of training vision models on massive internet datasets, train them only on varied sensor data from the one place where they'll actually work.
lead: Today, vision models train on millions of images from the internet to work anywhere. But most real machines operate in a single building, warehouse, or robot. This paper asks: what if you collected video, images, depth, sound, and other sensor streams from just your deployment space and trained only on that? You can match or beat giant internet-trained models without any external data.

problem.h2: Why Generalist Models Waste Power on Environments You'll Never See
paras: Today's computer vision models are trained as generalists. They learn from hundreds of millions of images on the internet, all mixed together—snowy mountains, beaches, cities, forests, animals. The goal is to build one model that works everywhere. But here is the waste: a robot deployed in a single warehouse learns to recognize objects it will never encounter. A camera system in one factory learns about tropical animals and ocean scenes. All that training on irrelevant data burns compute and GPU time.

A beginner might ask: why not just train a model on the few thousand images from my warehouse using supervised learning, with hand-labeled boxes and names? This breaks because supervised learning demands manual labels—time and money. And even with labels, a small dataset starves the model. It overfits, meaning it memorizes the exact pixels instead of learning general rules. It fails on lighting changes, new angles, or tiny shifts in the scene.

callout.html: Generalist models waste training on irrelevant places. Supervised learning on your space needs hand-labels and fails anyway.

steps.b: Collect multimodal data in your test space
steps.text: Cameras, depth sensors, audio, motion. No labels. Just raw streams from one place.

steps.b: Train by predicting one modality from another
steps.text: If I see the RGB image, predict the depth map. If I hear the sound, predict motion. No external data.
Because all modalities come from the same space, the model discovers what actually matters there.

steps.b: Specialize the weights to that single deployment
steps.text: Frozen model, but its internal detectors are now tuned to this warehouse, factory, or home.
Semantic segmentation, object detection, image captioning—all within this space.

paras: The paper moves the entire pre-training process from the internet into the test environment. Instead of downloading millions of images and training once, you collect a mix of modalities (images, depth, sound, haptics, motion) from the single place where the model will work, then train a fresh model on only that data.
object.object: Pre-training location: internet to test environment

hidden.h2: The Hidden Quantity: Cross-Modal Alignment Strength
hidden.name: Cross-modal alignment strength
paras: Alignment strength measures how reliably one modality predicts another. When an RGB image reliably predicts the depth map in your warehouse, the model's representation must capture the structure of that warehouse. High alignment means the two modalities genuinely share information because they come from the same place. Low alignment means the prediction task is too hard and the model learns generic features that work for any scene.

The paper estimates alignment implicitly: by training the model to predict depth from images, predict motion from sound, or predict surface normals from RGB, it forces the representation to absorb whatever shared structure exists. If the warehouse is consistent (good lighting, predictable layouts, stable scenes), cross-modal alignment is strong, and the model learns warehouse-specific features. If the data is chaotic, alignment is weak, and the model learns broad features.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger cross-modal prediction within the test space. Strongest pairs (image-depth-normals) build the representation.

reads.html: Alignment is simply: how well can you predict one sensor's output from another? Strong alignment means they carry the same information about the place.

The paper measures alignment implicitly by the downstream task performance (semantic segmentation, detection, captioning on held-out test images). Strong alignment leads to high downstream accuracy because when the representation has learned to predict depth from images, it has built internal filters that detect surfaces, edges, and spatial layout—exactly the features needed to label pixels by semantic category or detect objects.

paras: A vision model trained on millions of images learns reliable features because variety teaches general rules. A tiny warehouse dataset fails because the model sees the same walls and objects over and over and memorizes them. But here is the key: if you also capture depth, sound, and motion in that warehouse, you suddenly have variety—not of places, but of perspectives on the same place. The RGB camera sees a surface one way; the depth sensor sees it as a distance measurement; the audio captures echoes that reveal room shape; motion sensors reveal how objects move.

When the model is trained to predict depth from RGB, it must learn what parts of an image correspond to distance. When it predicts motion from sound, it must learn how vibrations encode object movement. Each cross-modal prediction task forces the model to extract a different slice of the warehouse's structure. Together, these slices build a specialized representation that would normally require millions of diverse images to learn. The model never memorizes pixels because the prediction targets (depth, motion, sound) are not pixel patterns—they are structural properties of the place.

This is why multimodal data from one space beats internet data trained on an irrelevant space. Internet data is broad but not deep in the target space. Multimodal data is narrow but dense in the target space. The model absorbs the warehouse's structure from multiple angles and builds detectors tuned to what matters there.

stages.s: Raw warehouse data: RGB images, depth maps, audio, motion, surface normals
Shared encoder learns features that align across modalities
Features are now tuned to the warehouse structure
Specialized representation ready for segmentation, detection, or captioning

math.words: Total loss equals the sum of individual cross-modal prediction losses. Each loss measures how well the model predicts one modality from another. Stronger predictions (lower loss) mean the representation has captured shared structure.
symbols: Prediction error when predicting depth from RGB image
Prediction error when predicting RGB from depth
Prediction error when predicting motion vectors from RGB
Prediction error when predicting motion from audio
Sum of all prediction errors; training minimizes this

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the model tries to predict depth from an RGB image of a warehouse shelf. Prediction error: 0.12 meters average. L_RGB_to_Depth = 0.12.
Predicting RGB from depth (reverse): error 25 pixel-units. L_Depth_to_RGB = 25.
Predicting motion from images: error 0.8 pixels per frame. L_RGB_to_Motion = 0.8.
Predicting motion from audio vibrations: error 1.2 pixels per frame. L_Audio_to_Motion = 1.2.
Total loss = 0.12 + 25 + 0.8 + 1.2 = 27.12. Training nudges the model to shrink all four errors. After training, total loss might drop to 8.5, meaning all cross-modal predictions improved.

math.note: Each modality pair teaches the model a different structural property of the warehouse; minimizing all losses together builds a representation tuned to that place.

charts.title: Internet-trained generalist (DINOv2)
charts.note: Strong across the internet, but not tuned to this warehouse.

charts.title: Test-Space Training (TST)
charts.note: Trained only on warehouse data but outperforms the generalist on this space because the representation learned to predict depth, motion, and other modalities—forcing it to build filters for the warehouse's specific structure, surfaces, and lighting—rather than learning generic features from unrelated internet scenes.

items.b: Test space is too small or repetitive.
items.html: If your warehouse is a single hallway with identical walls, cross-modal alignment is weak because there is little structure to learn. The depth map and RGB image predict each other trivially. The model learns almost nothing.

If you capture only RGB and depth but the task requires understanding motion (e.g., a moving conveyor belt), the representation misses that structural signal. Performance drops because the representation is incomplete.

If you train on the warehouse in summer but deploy in winter (different lighting, snow on windows), the specialized model fails. The features were tuned to one snapshot in time, not the full range of conditions.

Capture diverse modalities (RGB, depth, audio, motion, thermal if available) over weeks or months in the real deployment space, capturing seasonal and temporal shifts. The representation learns reliable warehouse-specific features that generalize within that space.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Collect multimodal data (RGB video, aligned depth, motion streams, audio) from a single room or warehouse for one hour. Divide into pre-training and test splits. Train a vision transformer using cross-modal prediction (RGB to depth, depth to RGB, motion prediction from frames). Then freeze the model and evaluate it on held-out test images from the same room, measuring semantic segmentation accuracy (how many pixels are correctly labeled). Compare against a model trained on large internet datasets like ImageNet. The demo is successful if test-space training matches or beats the internet-trained baseline.
demo.closing: The demo reveals that multimodality from one place teaches what million-image diversity from irrelevant places cannot: deep tuning to a specific deployment environment.
